title: Thomists: sufficient grace gives proximate and complete power
source_text: XXVI. Quamvis autem gratia quam ab efficaci distinguunt, non complectatur istud ultimum praerequisitum ad bene agendum, nihilominus pertendunt illam recte sufficientem dici: quia licet non sufficiat ut aliquis actu operetur, dat tamen vires bene operandi, & ad hoc sufficit ut quis bene operari possit. Imo vero per ejusmodi gratiam sufficientem dicunt non simpliciter dari bene agendi potentiam, sed potentiam talem quae mereatur dici proxima & completa; quanquam, ipsis fatentibus, novum Dei auxilium necessario bonam actionem praecedere debeat. Quemadmodum homo sanus cujus oculi sunt bene constituti, etiamsi in tenebris degat, habet ex ipsorum sensu, potentiam videndi proximam & completam, quanquam ad hoc ut visio fiat, praeter oculos bene constitutos, necessario requiratur lumen, quod praesentia objecta illustret.
pass_a_gloss: XXVI. But although the grace which they distinguish from efficacious, does not embrace that last prerequisite for acting well, nevertheless they maintain that it is rightly called sufficient; because although it does not suffice that someone work in act, yet it gives strengths of working well, and suffices for this that one can work well. Nay indeed through such sufficient grace they say there is given not simply the power of acting well, but power such as deserves to be called proximate and complete; although, they themselves confessing, a new help of God must necessarily precede the good action. Just as a healthy man whose eyes are well constituted, even if he pass time in darkness, has in their sense, the proximate and complete power of seeing, although for this that vision occur, besides eyes well constituted, light is necessarily required, which illuminates the present objects.
pass_b_english: Thesis XXVI. Although the grace they distinguish from efficacious grace does not include that final requirement for doing good, they still insist it is rightly called sufficient. It may not suffice for anyone actually to act, but it gives the strength to act well and suffices to make a person able to act well. Indeed they say such sufficient grace confers not just some power to do good, but a power that deserves to be called proximate and complete, even though, as they admit, a fresh aid from God must necessarily come before the good action.

Just so, a healthy person with sound eyes has, on their view, proximate and complete power to see even while he stays in darkness, although for sight actually to happen he needs, besides sound eyes, light to illuminate the objects before him.

lemmas.gloss: such as deserves to be called proximate and complete

choices.why: Scholastic terms for a power immediately ready to act; kept literal throughout the locus.
